name.text: Even and Odd Functions — combining two functions of known parity

questiontext.text:
Suppose \(f\) is an {@f_parity@} function and \(g\) is an {@g_parity@} function (both defined for all real numbers).

What can you say about the function [[if test="is(op=0)"]]\(h(x) = f(x) + g(x)\)[[else]]\(h(x) = f(x) \times g(x)\)[[/if]]?

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Work from the definitions: a function is even if \(f(-x) = f(x)\) and odd if \(f(-x) = -f(x)\). Replace \(x\) by \(-x\) in \(h\), use what you know about \(f\) and \(g\), and compare the result with \(h(x)\) and \(-h(x)\).

Here \(f\) is {@f_parity@} and \(g\) is {@g_parity@}, so \[ h(-x) = {@hnegdef@} = {@hneg@}. \]

[[if test="h_even"]]

This is exactly \(h(x)\), so \(h\) is always even.

[[elif test="h_odd"]]

This is exactly \(-h(x)\), so \(h\) is always odd.

[[else]]

This is in general neither \(h(x)\) nor \(-h(x)\), so \(h\) need not be even or odd. For example, \(x^2 + x\) is the sum of the even function \(x^2\) and the odd function \(x\), and it is neither even nor odd. (In a special case, such as when one of the functions is the zero function, the sum can still be even or odd, which is why the answer is "could be neither".)

[[/if]]

In summary, for sums: even + even is even, odd + odd is odd, and even + odd is in general neither. For products: even \(\times\) even is even, odd \(\times\) odd is even, and even \(\times\) odd is odd, just like multiplying signs.
